issues.note: A thin post-Thanksgiving window with no ED drug RCTs and almost nothing from the core EM or pharmacy journals, so this issue runs 8 picks led by observational work. The EM items are an Ontario survey of hyaluronidase stocking, an OPTPRESS septic shock secondary analysis, a pediatric anaphylaxis epinephrine series, a snakebite coagulopathy cohort and a case against routine benzonatate. A COMBINE-AF patient-level meta-analysis, a factor XIa inhibitor meta-analysis and a psychiatric ADR study round it out.
bottom_line: Only about 20% of Ontario hospitals stocked hyaluronidase on site, even though filler-induced vascular occlusion (skin necrosis, sudden vision loss) needs it within minutes. Check whether your ED can get it fast, or has a defined route to a site that can.

In 57,600 AF trial patients, DOACs beat warfarin for stroke and major bleeding whether or not aspirin was added, but aspirin on top raised both stroke and bleeding hazards. Ask why any anticoagulated patient is also on aspirin, and deprescribe when there's no clear indication.

Benzonatate has weak evidence for acute cough and real harms, including fast, fatal overdose in young children. Leave it off reflexive ED cough discharges, and if prescribed, counsel on locked storage.

articles.takeaway: Only 1 in 5 Ontario hospitals stocked hyaluronidase for filler-related vascular occlusion emergencies
articles.title: Provincial Assessment of Hyaluronidase Availability in Ontario Emergency Departments for the Treatment of Hyaluronic Acid Filler-Induced Vascular Occlusion.
articles.population: 197 of 205 Ontario public hospitals and affiliated sites (126 with an ED), phone survey of pharmacy or administrative staff, Mar–Jul 2025
articles.summary: Investigators asked each hospital whether hyaluronidase was on formulary and how many vials were on hand. Just 40 of 197 sites (20%) had it on site, most with only 1–5 vials; 8 relied on a partner hospital and 4 couldn't say how much they held. The study measured availability only, not patient outcomes or time to treatment.
articles.why: Cosmetic filler complications are rising and patients go to the nearest ED, where hyaluronidase may be the only treatment that can reverse an occlusion. ED pharmacists can review stocking (or a rapid-transfer pathway), keep a dosing reference with the antidote list and flag visual symptoms as an ophthalmology emergency.

articles.takeaway: Slow time to MAP target in older septic shock patients predicted death mainly when lactate was high
articles.title: Effect modification by baseline lactate in the association between time to assigned mean arterial pressure target and outcomes in older patients with septic shock: a post hoc analysis of the OPTPRESS trial.
articles.population: 472 older adults with septic shock from the OPTPRESS trial of MAP targets, multicenter in Japan
articles.summary: The authors measured how long it took each patient to first reach their randomized MAP target and tested whether baseline lactate changed how that time related to outcomes. The interaction was significant: patients with high lactate and a slow time to target had higher 90-day and 28-day mortality and fewer ventilator-free and dialysis-free days than those with low lactate and a fast response. A slow response with low lactate carried no excess risk. Results held after adjusting for pre-randomization norepinephrine dose, but the analysis is hypothesis-generating.
articles.why: A patient who stays below MAP target despite climbing norepinephrine and has a high lactate is the one to escalate early. ED pharmacists can prompt timely vasopressin, hydrocortisone and a reassessment of source and fluids instead of waiting at the same norepinephrine dose.

articles.takeaway: IM epinephrine was given first-line in 79% of pediatric anaphylaxis cases, with no adverse reactions in 171 children
articles.title: Clinical characteristics and adrenaline use in anaphylaxis in children: a cross-sectional study.
articles.population: 115 children with anaphylaxis plus 70 given IM epinephrine for non-anaphylaxis reasons, 1 children's hospital in Hangzhou, China, 2021–2024
articles.summary: Foods (45%) and drugs (30%) were the main triggers, and nearly all children had skin and respiratory involvement. IM epinephrine was given to 88% of anaphylaxis patients and as first-line treatment in 79%, so about 1 in 5 got something else first. No adverse reactions were recorded after IM epinephrine in either the anaphylaxis group or the 70 children who received it without anaphylaxis. The authors highlight both delayed use in true anaphylaxis and overuse as prophylaxis.
articles.why: Supports giving IM epinephrine (0.01 mg/kg of 1 mg/mL, max 0.3 mg in children, into the thigh) without hesitation when anaphylaxis is suspected; antihistamines and steroids shouldn't come first. Pharmacists can keep weight-based dosing visible and prescribe two auto-injectors at discharge.

articles.takeaway: Each hour of delay after a hemotoxic snakebite raised the odds of consumptive coagulopathy by about 5%
articles.title: Risk factors for venom-induced consumption coagulopathy after snakebite in Yunnan, China: a multicenter retrospective study.
articles.population: 801 patients bitten by predominantly hemotoxic snakes and seen within 24 hours, 21 hospitals in Yunnan, China (Yunnan Snakebite Injury Database)
articles.summary: VICC on admission (INR over 1.2 plus low fibrinogen or very high D-dimer, before treatment) was present in 14%. Ovophis bites carried much higher odds than Trimeresurus bites (aOR 7.65), and each extra hour from bite to hospital raised the odds by 5% (aOR 1.05). Some first-aid practices also showed associations, but the authors warn these may be confounded.
articles.why: The species are Asian, but the lesson carries over to US pit viper bites: coagulopathy develops with time, so get patients in fast, check INR, fibrinogen and platelets on arrival and repeat them, and have antivenom (CroFab or Anavip) dosing worked out early. Avoid tourniquets and other unproven first aid.

articles.study_type: Clinical review (Things We Do for No Reason)
articles.takeaway: Benzonatate has little evidence for acute cough and real risks, including fatal overdose
articles.title: Things We Do for No Reason™: Routine use of benzonatate for acute cough suppression.
articles.population: Review of efficacy and safety evidence for benzonatate in hospitalized and acute-care adults
articles.summary: The authors find no modern RCTs showing that benzonatate meaningfully improves patient-centered cough outcomes. In contrast, published reports describe hypersensitivity reactions, neuropsychiatric effects and rare but potentially fatal overdoses. They argue that its low cost and non-opioid image don't justify routine use.
articles.why: Benzonatate is a common ED cough discharge, yet overdose can cause seizures, dysrhythmias and cardiac arrest within an hour, and young children are especially at risk from swallowing or chewing capsules. Pharmacists can steer toward honey (over age 1), time and treating the cause, and counsel on child-safe storage when it's prescribed.

articles.takeaway: DOACs beat warfarin with or without aspirin in AF, but adding aspirin raised both stroke and bleeding
articles.title: Direct Oral Anticoagulants Versus Warfarin According to Antiplatelet Therapy Use in Atrial Fibrillation: A Patient-Level Meta-Analysis of 4 Randomized Trials From COMBINE-AF.
articles.population: 57,598 patients with AF from the 4 pivotal DOAC vs warfarin trials; 34% on baseline antiplatelet therapy (over 90% aspirin alone)
articles.summary: Patients on antiplatelet therapy had higher adjusted hazards of stroke or systemic embolism (HR 1.17) and major bleeding (HR 1.38) regardless of treatment arm. DOACs reduced stroke or embolism (HR 0.85 without and 0.77 with antiplatelets) and major bleeding (HR 0.85 and 0.88) to a similar degree in both groups, along with consistent cuts in fatal and intracranial bleeding. GI bleeding was higher with DOACs, especially in older patients also on antiplatelets.
articles.why: Supports a DOAC over warfarin for AF whether or not the patient needs an antiplatelet. When an anticoagulated patient comes to the ED with a GI bleed, check for aspirin with no clear indication (such as remote stable CAD) and flag it for deprescribing at discharge.

articles.takeaway: Factor XIa inhibitors cut strokes by about 23% without a significant rise in major bleeding
articles.title: Factor XIa Inhibitors and Stroke Prevention: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials Including the Phase 3 OCEANIC-STROKE Trial.
articles.population: 5 RCTs, 18,857 participants, including the phase 3 OCEANIC-STROKE trial of asundexian
articles.summary: Pooled across trials, factor XIa inhibitors reduced any stroke (RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.68–0.87). Major bleeding wasn't significantly higher (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.89–1.37), and major cardiovascular events and mortality trended lower. The abstract gives few details on the comparators or which agents and indications were pooled.
articles.why: Asundexian and milvexian are heading toward use for secondary stroke prevention on top of antiplatelets. Note that asundexian was less effective than apixaban in AF (OCEANIC-AF), so these aren't a DOAC swap, and ED pharmacists should prepare for reversal questions since no specific antidote exists yet.

articles.takeaway: Over a third of psychiatric inpatient transfers to a general hospital were drug reactions, and most were preventable
articles.title: Adverse Drug Reaction Requiring Transfer of Psychiatric Inpatients to a General Hospital: The IATROPSY Study.
articles.population: 114 transfers from 2,782 psychiatric hospital stays to a general hospital, France, Feb–Jul 2024
articles.summary: A drug safety specialist reviewed every transfer, and 43 (38%) were linked to adverse drug reactions. Neurological effects (confusion, altered consciousness, sedation, seizures) and falls were the most common, and antipsychotics (63%) and anxiolytics or hypnotics (35%) were the main culprits. Two independent reviewers judged 58% preventable or potentially preventable, mostly due to doses above the approved label.
articles.why: Psychiatric patients sent to the ED for confusion, oversedation, falls or seizures often have a drug cause. Review recent antipsychotic and benzodiazepine dose escalations, check for anticholinergic burden, QTc and sodium, and consider NMS or serotonin toxicity before attributing symptoms to the psychiatric illness.

issues.note: A very thin Thanksgiving window with no ED drug RCTs, so this issue runs short at 6 picks rather than padding. The EM items are a Swedish cohort on opioids given before in-hospital cardiac arrest, a meta-analysis of IV lytics in stroke patients on DOACs and a review of cipepofol, the propofol alternative FDA-approved in May 2026. A CRRT phosphate RCT, an asymptomatic bacteriuria meta-analysis and a metformin–B12 neuropathy meta-analysis round it out.
bottom_line: 40% of in-hospital cardiac arrest patients had been given an opioid in the prior 24 hours (16% within 2 hours), yet naloxone was used in only 2% of arrests. Any exposure wasn't linked to outcomes, but higher cumulative doses were tied to lower ROSC, so check the MAR during inpatient and boarder codes.

Observational data across 9,500 DOAC-exposed stroke patients found no rise in symptomatic ICH with IV lytics, but guidelines still say avoid unless the last dose was over 48 hours ago or drug levels are low. Pharmacists should pin down the agent and last dose time fast so the team can apply local criteria.

Asymptomatic bacteriuria treatment helped in pregnancy and before urologic procedures but not in kidney transplant recipients, and only modestly reduced UTI in institutionalized older adults. ED urine cultures without symptoms still mostly shouldn't lead to antibiotics.

articles.takeaway: Two in five in-hospital arrest patients got an opioid in the prior 24 hours, but naloxone was rarely given
articles.title: Opioid administration prior to in-hospital cardiac arrest.
articles.population: 267 adult in-hospital cardiac arrests, 9 hospitals in southern Sweden, 2024
articles.summary: Medical records were checked for opioids given in the 24 hours before arrest. 40% of patients had received one (16% within the last 2 hours), at a modest median cumulative dose of 17 oral MME, with the last dose a median 2.7 hours before arrest. Naloxone was given in only 6 arrests (2%). Any opioid exposure wasn't associated with ROSC (OR 1.03) or 30-day survival (OR 0.98), but each step up in cumulative dose was linked to slightly lower odds of ROSC (OR 0.91, p = 0.04). Small sample, exploratory analyses.
articles.why: Guidelines allow naloxone in suspected opioid-associated arrest, but routine use during IHCA isn't proven. ED pharmacists responding to codes on boarders can quickly review recent opioid, sedative and PCA doses, and naloxone 0.4–2 mg IV is reasonable when respiratory arrest preceded the pulse loss.

articles.takeaway: IV lytics in stroke patients recently on a DOAC didn't raise symptomatic brain bleeding vs non-anticoagulated patients
articles.title: Safety and Efficacy of Intravenous Thrombolysis after DOAC Use in Acute Ischemic Stroke: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis in Light of Current Guidelines.
articles.population: 11 comparative studies, 262,325 patients with acute ischemic stroke given IV thrombolysis, 9,497 with prior DOAC use
articles.summary: Symptomatic ICH (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.79–1.29), any ICH (RR 1.47, 95% CI 0.77–2.83) and mortality (RR 0.63, not significant) didn't differ between DOAC-exposed and non-anticoagulated patients. DOAC users had more good 3-month outcomes (mRS 0–2; RR 2.43), likely reflecting selection, and more major extracranial bleeding (RR 1.62, 95% CI 1.18–2.21). All data were observational, with patients on DOACs carefully selected (e.g., by timing, levels or idarucizumab).
articles.why: Supports the growing practice of considering lytics in selected DOAC patients (e.g., last dose over 48 hours, low anti-Xa or dabigatran level, or after idarucizumab). The ED pharmacist's job is to confirm the agent, dose, last dose time and renal function within minutes so the stroke team isn't delayed.

articles.takeaway: Newly approved cipepofol works like propofol with less injection pain, but isn't proven safer overall
articles.title: Cipepofol Versus Propofol Across Adult Anaesthesia and Sedation: A Comprehensive Clinical Review of Pharmacology, Clinical Efficacy, Recovery, and Safety.
articles.population: 85 adult randomized comparisons of cipepofol (ciprofol) vs propofol: 41 general anesthesia, 40 procedural sedation, 4 ICU sedation
articles.summary: Cipepofol was FDA-approved in May 2026 for adult surgical induction only. Across trials it achieved high sedation and induction success, and direct comparisons consistently showed less injection pain than propofol. Hemodynamic and respiratory effects varied with dose, population and how events were defined, and recovery results were mixed. No benefit on cognition, organ protection, mortality or rare harms was shown, and there was no formal meta-analysis or bias assessment.
articles.why: Expect formulary questions about cipepofol for ED procedural sedation, which is off-label for now. It's dosed far lower per kg than propofol (roughly 0.3–0.5 mg/kg for induction), so pharmacists should guard against mg-for-mg substitution errors and keep the same monitoring standards.

articles.takeaway: Phosphate-containing CRRT replacement fluid cut hypophosphatemia from 69% to 16% but caused some hypoglycemia
articles.title: Phosphate-containing versus phosphate-free replacement solution in critically ill patients requiring continuous renal replacement therapy: a randomized controlled trial.
articles.population: 90 critically ill adults starting CRRT, several ICUs in China
articles.summary: Patients were randomized to phosphate-containing or phosphate-free replacement solution. Hypophosphatemia in the first 48 hours occurred in 15.6% vs 68.9% (adjusted OR 0.05, 95% CI 0.01–0.18), and the phosphate group needed less supplementation. Hypoglycemia was more common with the phosphate solution (8.9% vs 0%), and some patients with high baseline phosphate developed hyperphosphatemia. Creatinine and SOFA scores didn't differ, and clinical outcomes weren't assessed.
articles.why: Relevant to toxicology and DKA/hyperkalemia patients who start CRRT while boarding. Pharmacists can push for phosphate-containing solutions or scheduled repletion, with glucose checks and avoidance in patients who are already hyperphosphatemic.

articles.takeaway: Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria helped in pregnancy and before urologic procedures, not in transplant recipients
articles.title: To treat or not to treat? A systematic review and updated meta-analysis on the management of asymptomatic bacteriuria.
articles.population: 48 studies, 6,477 patients: pregnant women, institutionalized older adults, kidney transplant recipients and endourology patients
articles.summary: In pregnancy, antibiotics reduced symptomatic UTI (OR 0.25) and preterm delivery (OR 0.30). Before endourological procedures they lowered postoperative UTI (OR 0.15). In institutionalized older adults, treatment reduced symptomatic UTI (OR 0.47) but didn't clear bacteriuria, and in kidney transplant recipients it had no effect on UTI, pyelonephritis, rejection or graft loss. Study designs and quality varied.
articles.why: Matches IDSA guidance: screen and treat only in pregnancy and before invasive urologic procedures. For confused older ED patients with a positive urinalysis and no urinary symptoms or sepsis, pharmacists can push back on reflexive antibiotics.

articles.takeaway: Metformin was linked to more peripheral neuropathy, and about a third of users had low B12
articles.title: Association of metformin use with vitamin B12 deficiency and peripheral neuropathy in type 2 diabetes mellitus: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.population: 20 observational studies, about 292,000 adults with type 2 diabetes in 15 countries
articles.summary: Pooled cross-sectional data linked metformin use to higher odds of peripheral neuropathy (OR 1.84, 95% CI 1.18–2.88; I² 69%), with supportive cohort estimates. B12 deficiency predicted neuropathy (OR 2.09) and affected 32% of metformin users at standard thresholds; one cohort found much higher risk when both were present (HR 5.76). The evidence is observational and heterogeneous.
articles.why: When a patient on long-term metformin presents with neuropathy, falls or unexplained macrocytic anemia, check a B12 level. ADA already recommends periodic B12 monitoring, and pharmacists can flag it during med reconciliation.

issues.note: The headliner is FISSH, a blinded Canadian-Saudi RCT of lactated Ringer's vs saline in septic shock, joined by a vasopressin-vs-norepinephrine meta-analysis and an AJEM review of xylazine, medetomidine and nitazenes. Three stroke pharmacotherapy papers (alteplase in minor stroke, early BP lowering in CATIS-2 and ticagrelor by frailty in CHANCE-2), a pediatric ED ketamine-for-agitation series and an NEJM blood pressure meta-analysis round out 8 picks.
bottom_line: Lactated Ringer's and saline gave identical 30-day mortality in septic shock (33.6% vs 33.0%) across about 5.8 L of study fluid. Either crystalloid is acceptable, so choose based on chloride, potassium and compatibility rather than expected survival benefit.

Pooled data put alteplase for minor, likely non-disabling stroke (mostly NIHSS 5 or below) at no functional benefit and about 6-fold higher symptomatic ICH. It supports holding lytics for non-disabling deficits and saving them for disabling ones.

Persistent sedation after naloxone, bradycardia or hypotension, or a severe hypertensive withdrawal points to medetomidine or xylazine in the drug supply. Titrate naloxone to breathing, not wakefulness, and expect routine screens to miss these agents.

articles.takeaway: Lactated Ringer's didn't lower 30-day mortality vs saline in septic shock
articles.title: Ringer's lactate versus saline in the fluids in septic shock (FISSH) trial: a multicentre, blinded, parallel-group, randomised controlled trial.
articles.population: 1,103 adults with septic shock enrolled within 6 hours of ED presentation or ICU consult, 30 hospitals in Canada and Saudi Arabia, 2018–2026
articles.summary: All bolus and maintenance fluid through the ICU stay (up to day 30) was blinded lactated Ringer's or 0.9% saline; patients were very sick (mean APACHE II about 25, lactate 4.8 mmol/L) and got about 5.8 L of study fluid. 30-day in-hospital mortality was 33.6% with Ringer's vs 33.0% with saline (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.86–1.21), and no serious adverse events were attributed to either fluid. Enrollment took more than 7 years, and patients with raised ICP or on dialysis were excluded.
articles.why: Joins BaSICS and PLUS in finding no mortality difference between balanced fluids and saline. ED pharmacists can let practical issues drive the choice: avoid large saline volumes in hyperchloremic acidosis, avoid Ringer's with ceftriaxone in the same line or in raised ICP, and focus on stopping fluids once perfusion recovers.

articles.takeaway: Vasopressin matched norepinephrine on mortality but cut dialysis, mainly when started first-line
articles.title: Vasopressin Versus Norepinephrine in Septic Shock: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Trials Focusing on Vasopressor Timing.
articles.population: 6 RCTs, 1,580 adults with septic shock randomized to vasopressin or norepinephrine
articles.summary: Short-term mortality didn't differ (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.86–1.11; I² 0%), and neither did serious adverse events or ICU stay. Renal replacement therapy was less common with vasopressin (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.72–0.97), and in subgroups the effect appeared when vasopressin was the first randomized agent (RR 0.65) but not when it was added second-line (RR 0.96). The RRT result relied on a fixed-effect model and the timing subgroup is exploratory.
articles.why: Norepinephrine stays first-line, but this supports adding vasopressin (fixed 0.03 units/min) early rather than as a last resort, typically once norepinephrine reaches about 0.25–0.5 mcg/kg/min, especially when AKI is developing. ED pharmacists can keep vasopressin available for boarding shock patients.

articles.takeaway: Xylazine, medetomidine and nitazenes cause naloxone-resistant sedation, bradycardia and recurrent respiratory depression
articles.title: Emerging designer sedatives and adulterants in the emergency department: A narrative review.
articles.population: Review of epidemiology, presentation and ED management of veterinary sedatives (xylazine, medetomidine) and novel synthetic opioids (nitazenes, orphine analogues) in the US drug supply
articles.summary: The alpha-2 agonists xylazine and medetomidine add deep sedation, bradycardia and hypotension to opioid overdoses and aren't reversed by naloxone. Xylazine causes chronic necrotic wounds, and medetomidine can cause prolonged toxicity and a severe withdrawal with hypertension, tachycardia and agitation. Nitazenes and orphine analogues are very potent mu-opioid agonists that can cause recurrent respiratory depression needing repeat naloxone or an infusion, and none of these agents shows up on routine hospital drug screens.
articles.why: Give naloxone for the opioid component, titrated to ventilation, then support airway and breathing rather than escalating naloxone for leftover sedation. Medetomidine withdrawal is a newer ED problem; it is often treated with dexmedetomidine or clonidine plus benzodiazepines, so involve poison control early.

articles.takeaway: Alteplase for minor stroke didn't improve function and raised symptomatic brain bleeding about 6-fold
articles.title: Alteplase in minor ischemic stroke: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized and prospective studies.
articles.population: 11 RCTs, RCT subgroups and prospective studies, 9,680 patients with minor ischemic stroke (mostly NIHSS 5 or below; 3,664 alteplase vs 6,016 control)
articles.summary: Excellent outcome (mRS 0–1) didn't differ with alteplase (OR 1.05, 95% CI 0.83–1.33), nor did functional independence or mortality. Symptomatic ICH was much higher (OR 6.01, 95% CI 2.60–13.89), as was any ICH (OR 1.86). A possible benefit was seen only in higher-risk minor-stroke subgroups. The review mixes randomized and observational data, doesn't clearly separate disabling from non-disabling deficits, and excludes tenecteplase.
articles.why: Consistent with PRISMS and ARAMIS: for minor, non-disabling strokes, dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus clopidogrel for 21 days) is usually preferred over lytics. Stroke pharmacists can help the team judge whether a low NIHSS deficit is actually disabling before mixing alteplase or tenecteplase.

articles.takeaway: Early BP lowering after non-lysed ischemic stroke raised recurrent strokes in moderate-to-severe cases
articles.title: Antihypertensive Treatment Timing and Clinical Outcomes in Acute Ischemic Stroke Without Reperfusion Therapy by Stroke Severity: A Subgroup Analysis of the CATIS-2 Trial.
articles.population: 4,802 patients with acute ischemic stroke, elevated SBP and no reperfusion therapy, randomized 24–48 hours after onset, China (3,263 minor, 1,539 moderate-to-severe)
articles.summary: Patients got antihypertensives immediately or starting on day 8. Death or disability at 90 days didn't differ by timing in minor (5.6% vs 4.3%) or moderate-to-severe stroke (26.1% vs 23.2%). In moderate-to-severe stroke, early treatment was linked to more recurrent strokes (8.3% vs 5.1%; OR 1.73), major vascular events and serious adverse events (9.9% vs 6.4%), with significant interactions. These are exploratory subgroup findings with multiple comparisons.
articles.why: For patients who didn't get lytics or thrombectomy, there's no rush to lower BP unless it exceeds about 220/120; permissive hypertension remains the default. This doesn't apply to post-lytic patients, who still need BP under 180/105.

articles.takeaway: Ketamine for severe agitation in a pediatric ED worked after one dose in 85% of episodes, with few adverse events
articles.title: Ketamine administration for acute severe agitation in a pediatric emergency department: prevalence and clinical profile-a 6-year retrospective study.
articles.population: 26 agitation episodes in 22 children (median age 16) among 139,295 visits, 1 tertiary pediatric ED in Trieste, Italy, 2020–2025
articles.summary: Agitation accounted for 1.3% of visits, and ketamine was used in 26 episodes, about 9% of all ketamine doses given in the ED; that share rose from zero to about 7.5% over the study. Ketamine was given IV in 65% and IM in 23% of episodes, a single dose controlled agitation in 85%, and adverse events were rare. Half of the patients went home from the ED and 27% were admitted to the ICU. The cohort is very small, with no comparison group.
articles.why: Ketamine is a reasonable rescue for dangerous agitation in adolescents when antipsychotics or benzodiazepines fail or would be too slow. Typical dosing is 1–2 mg/kg IV or 4–5 mg/kg IM; monitor for laryngospasm, hypersalivation and emergence reactions with airway equipment at the bedside.

articles.takeaway: Ticagrelor-aspirin beat clopidogrel-aspirin in CYP2C19 loss-of-function carriers, except in the most frail patients
articles.title: Ticagrelor-aspirin versus clopidogrel-aspirin by pre-onset frailty status: a subgroup analysis of the CHANCE-2 trial.
articles.population: 6,412 patients with minor ischemic stroke or TIA who carried CYP2C19 loss-of-function alleles, CHANCE-2 trial, China
articles.summary: Patients were split into tertiles of a frailty index built from pre-stroke deficits. Ticagrelor-aspirin reduced 90-day stroke in the least frail (HR 0.64, 95% CI 0.45–0.90) and middle (HR 0.68) tertiles but not the most frail (HR 1.05, 95% CI 0.76–1.44), with a significant interaction. Moderate or severe bleeding didn't differ by frailty. It's a post hoc analysis in a Chinese population, and absolute event rates weren't reported in the abstract.
articles.why: Where CYP2C19 testing is available, ticagrelor-based DAPT is the pick for poor clopidogrel metabolizers after minor stroke or TIA. In very frail older patients the benefit is uncertain, so clopidogrel-based DAPT or a shorter course is reasonable while weighing bleeding and dyspnea.

articles.takeaway: Each 5 mm Hg drop in systolic BP cut major cardiovascular events 10%, even at lowest baseline risk
articles.title: Blood-Pressure-Lowering Treatment across the Cardiovascular Risk Spectrum.
articles.population: 51 RCTs, 357,440 participants grouped into deciles of predicted 5-year cardiovascular risk (lowest under 4%, highest over 27%); BPLTTC
articles.summary: Over a median 4.2 years, each 5 mm Hg reduction in systolic BP lowered major cardiovascular events by about 10% (HR 0.90, 95% CI 0.88–0.92), with the same relative effect in every risk decile. Absolute benefit grew with risk: 5-year NNT was 255 in the lowest decile vs 38 in the highest. Treatment raised hypotension, bradycardia or palpitations (12.0 vs 6.5 per 1,000 person-years), renal events and falls, with a similar relative increase across risk levels.
articles.why: Supports treating hypertension on BP alone, not just high calculated risk. For ED patients with asymptomatic elevated BP, the job is to arrange outpatient follow-up rather than rapid lowering, and to watch for falls and hypotension in older adults on several antihypertensives.

issues.note: The headliners are the twin PITSTOP trials in JAMA, which randomized Ontario paramedics' sepsis patients to ambulance ceftriaxone and to liberal fluids. Other EM items are an Edinburgh acetaminophen hepatotoxicity score, a meta-analysis on restarting anticoagulation for AF after ICH, a 62-trial sepsis landscape review and a pediatric sedation RCT. A large postoperative opioid cohort and a pharmacist-led SGLT2 inhibitor program round out 8 picks.
bottom_line: Giving IM ceftriaxone in the ambulance, about 3.5 hours before ED antibiotics, didn't lower hospital mortality in hypotensive febrile sepsis (18.0% vs 18.4%). Prehospital antibiotics aren't a priority for EMS protocols, but the first ED dose should still go in fast.
An extra 900 mL of prehospital saline didn't change sepsis mortality either (18.0% vs 18.3%), and pulmonary edema was rare. Smaller, SBP-guided boluses are a reasonable default before arrival.

Restarting oral anticoagulation in AF patients who survived an ICH cut major cardiovascular events by about 40% across 5 small RCTs. Pharmacists can push for a documented restart plan rather than indefinite holding.

articles.takeaway: Ceftriaxone given in the ambulance didn't lower sepsis mortality compared with waiting for ED antibiotics
articles.title: Prehospital Antibiotics for Patients With Suspected Sepsis: The PITSTOP-Antibiotics Factorial Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.population: 2,048 adults with suspected infection, fever of 38 °C or higher and SBP under 100 mm Hg (median age 75), 4 paramedic services in Ontario, Canada, 2020–2025
articles.summary: Paramedics gave 1 g of IM ceftriaxone or placebo a mean of about 38 minutes after reaching the patient, and more than 92% in both groups got open-label antibiotics in hospital roughly 4 hours after paramedic arrival. Hospital mortality to day 90 was 18.0% with ceftriaxone vs 18.4% with placebo (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.81–1.17). None of the 17 secondary outcomes, including ICU admission, ventilation, dialysis and positive cultures, differed.
articles.why: A 3-hour head start on a single dose made no difference, which tempers the 'every minute counts' message for undifferentiated suspected sepsis. It doesn't change the goal of antibiotics within 1 hour for septic shock in the ED, and a prehospital dose shouldn't stop cultures or the full ED regimen.

articles.takeaway: Up to 2 L of saline in the ambulance didn't improve sepsis survival over SBP-guided usual care
articles.title: Prehospital Fluid Resuscitation for Patients With Suspected Sepsis: The PITSTOP-Fluids Factorial Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.population: 1,646 adults with suspected infection, fever and SBP under 100 mm Hg with IV access (median age 76), 4 paramedic services in Ontario, Canada, 2020–2025
articles.summary: The liberal arm got up to 2 L of normal saline regardless of later blood pressure, while usual care gave fluid only for SBP under 90 and stopped at 100. Median prehospital volume was 1,500 mL vs 500 mL (difference about 910 mL). Hospital mortality was 18.0% vs 18.3% (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.80–1.20), all 17 secondary outcomes were similar, and pulmonary edema during transport was infrequent in both groups.
articles.why: Adds to CLOVERS-era evidence that more early fluid isn't better. In the ED, count prehospital volume toward the 30 mL/kg target, reassess before giving more, and start norepinephrine early (peripherally if needed) when hypotension persists.

articles.takeaway: A score using routine admission labs flagged acetaminophen overdoses likely to get liver injury despite acetylcysteine
articles.title: Prediction of Acetaminophen-Induced Hepatotoxicity in Acetylcysteine-Treated Patients Using Routine Admission Biomarkers.
articles.population: 4,705 acetaminophen overdose admissions aged 12 and older with admission ALT of 1,000 U/L or less, 3 UK hospitals, 2008–2024
articles.summary: Hepatotoxicity (peak ALT over 1,000 U/L) developed in 2.5% despite acetylcysteine. The Edinburgh Risk Score uses four routine labs per stratum: acetaminophen level, sodium, potassium and lymphocytes when ALT is 50 or below, and ALT, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase and lymphocytes when ALT is 51–1,000. In a held-out test set its AUC was 0.93 vs 0.82 for an acetaminophen-aminotransferase product over 1,500, with specificity of 83% vs 63% and about half as many false-positive escalations. It still needs external validation.
articles.why: Identifying high-risk patients early is what decides who gets intensified therapy, such as higher-dose acetylcysteine, fomepizole or extracorporeal removal for massive ingestions. Until this is validated, keep using the nomogram and AT product with poison center input.

articles.takeaway: Restarting oral anticoagulation for AF after a brain bleed cut major cardiovascular events by about 40%
articles.title: Efficacy and Safety of Oral Anticoagulation for Atrial Fibrillation after Intracerebral Hemorrhage: A Systematic Review and Frequentist-Bayesian Meta-Analysis.
articles.population: 5 RCTs, 733 adults with atrial fibrillation after spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage, starting oral anticoagulation vs none
articles.summary: Oral anticoagulation was associated with fewer major adverse cardiovascular events than no anticoagulation (RR 0.59, 95% CI 0.37–0.94; I² 24%). Bayesian analyses also favored anticoagulation across most prior and heterogeneity assumptions, with more than a 90% probability of at least a 20% relative reduction in 6 of 10 scenarios. The total sample was small, so the estimate for recurrent ICH is less certain.
articles.why: Many ICH survivors with AF are left off anticoagulation indefinitely. When an ICH patient on a DOAC comes in, reversal is the immediate job, but pharmacists can also flag the need for a documented restart plan (typically a DOAC, often weeks after the bleed) before discharge.

articles.takeaway: Across 62 sepsis RCTs, no treatment domain (fluids, vasopressors, steroids, vitamin C) reliably lowered mortality
articles.title: The sepsis trial landscape: a domain-specific systematic review and meta-analysis of adult sepsis randomized controlled trials.
articles.population: 62 adult sepsis and septic shock RCTs, 2000–2025, 36,739 patients
articles.summary: Trials were grouped into six domains. Pooled mortality risk ratios were 0.88 for resuscitation strategies, 0.96 for fluid quantity, 0.95 for fluid type, 0.97 for vasopressors, 0.92 for corticosteroids (95% CI 0.84–1.00) and 0.95 for vitamin C regimens, none clearly significant. Small trials scattered widely while large trials clustered near no effect, and the authors point to late intervention timing, patient heterogeneity, contamination and infrastructure limits as recurring design problems.
articles.why: Explains why sepsis care still rests on basics: source control, timely appropriate antibiotics and supportive care. Steroids come closest to benefit, consistent with hydrocortisone for patients on ongoing vasopressors.

articles.takeaway: Propofol-ketamine sped recovery by about 1 minute and cut emergence delirium vs mask sevoflurane for pediatric MRI
articles.title: Two Anesthetic Strategies for Pediatric Magnetic Resonance Imaging: Face-Mask Sevoflurane Versus an Intravenous Propofol-Ketamine Regimen in a Randomized Parallel-Group Trial.
articles.population: 211 children aged 3 months to 10 years having MRI under anesthesia, 1 center
articles.summary: Children got IV ketamine-propofol induction with intermittent propofol boluses or face-mask sevoflurane maintenance. Recovery was slightly faster with propofol-ketamine (4.5 vs 5.3 minutes; trimmed difference about 1 minute) and peak emergence delirium scores were lower, but extra anesthetic was needed more often (29% vs 11%). Discharge time, image quality, and respiratory and hemodynamic events didn't differ.
articles.why: Supports ketofol-style regimens for pediatric procedural sedation, with less emergence agitation than volatile agents. Expect to need top-up propofol doses, and draw them up ahead of time with weight-based limits.

articles.takeaway: Discharge opioids of 50 MME a day or more, especially beyond 14 days, were tied to earlier opioid use disorder
articles.title: Early post-discharge opioid prescribing and opioid use disorder after surgery: multicentre electronic health record cohort study.
articles.population: 6,113,697 procedures in patients 12 and older across 57 procedures and 13 surgical departments, US health systems (Oracle Health Real-World Data), 2012–2024
articles.summary: Incident OUD within a year occurred in about 5 per 1,000 surgical patients vs about 1.9 per 1,000 in a comparator without these procedures, peaking 1–2 months after discharge and highest in patients with cancer or chronic pain. High-dose prescriptions (50 MME/day or more), particularly lasting more than 14 days, were associated with a shorter time to an OUD diagnosis across departments (time ratios 0.79–0.94). It's observational and relies on recorded diagnoses.
articles.why: The same dose-and-duration logic applies to ED discharge prescriptions: keep daily MME low, limit supply to a few days, pair with scheduled acetaminophen and NSAIDs, and offer naloxone when doses climb.

articles.takeaway: A centralized pharmacist program got half of eligible patients on SGLT2 inhibitors, with 27% fewer hospitalizations or deaths
articles.title: Clinical Pharmacist-Supported Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter 2 Inhibitor Initiation and Patient Outcomes in Primary Care.
articles.population: 1,965 SGLT2 inhibitor-eligible patients identified by clinical pharmacists in a nationwide HMO, 2020–2023
articles.summary: Clinical pharmacists screened the EHR and sent initiation recommendations to primary care physicians; 48% of eligible patients started an SGLT2 inhibitor within a year. In time-dependent analyses, starting one was associated with lower risk of all-cause hospitalization or death (aHR 0.73, 95% CI 0.58–0.92), with 18.2 vs 23.5 events per 100 person-years. Initiators may have differed from non-initiators in ways the models didn't capture.
articles.why: A practical model for pharmacist-driven guideline therapy. In the ED, remember SGLT2 inhibitors when evaluating euglycemic DKA, volume depletion and genital infections, and advise holding them during acute illness or before procedures.

issues.note: A thin Monday window with no ED drug RCTs, so this issue runs short at 7 picks rather than padding. The EM items are a London cohort on DOACs and brain bleeds after head injury, a ceftriaxone vs cefazolin-plus-aminoglycoside comparison for type III open fractures, CRRT clearance in diquat poisoning and a 10-hospital sepsis decision-support study. The 1-year AID-ICU haloperidol follow-up, a primary care stewardship program and a dupilumab cardiovascular signal round it out.
bottom_line: Among 11,400 head-injured adults who got a CT in three London EDs, DOAC users had no more acute intracranial hemorrhage than non-anticoagulated patients (7.1% vs 7.7%; aOR 0.93). It supports a less reflexive approach to DOAC head injuries, but reversal agents should still be ready when a bleed is found.

Ceftriaxone alone had a similar surgical site infection rate to cefazolin plus an aminoglycoside for type III open fractures (12% vs 17%) in a small cohort, with no AKI difference. That makes a single once-daily drug a reasonable option where local guidance allows.

A sepsis navigation tool (real-time timer, order set shortcuts) was followed by about 27% lower adjusted odds of death or hospice across 10 hospitals, along with faster cultures and antibiotics. It's quasi-experimental, but it shows workflow design moves sepsis outcomes.

articles.takeaway: DOAC users had no more brain bleeding on CT after head injury than patients on no anticoagulant
articles.title: Direct Oral Anticoagulant Use and Acute Intracranial Hemorrhage in Adults Undergoing CT After Head Injury.
articles.population: 11,401 head CT episodes in 10,625 adults with head injury (565 on a DOAC), 3 EDs in one London NHS trust, 2018–2022
articles.summary: Linked ED, hospital and primary care prescribing records compared patients with an active DOAC prescription to those on no anticoagulant. Acute intracranial hemorrhage on the first CT occurred in 7.1% of DOAC episodes vs 7.7% of the others, and the adjusted odds weren't higher (aOR 0.93, 95% CI 0.70–1.21). Neurosurgery was rare in both groups (0.4%), and although crude 28-day mortality was higher with DOACs (3.0% vs 1.7%), it wasn't after adjustment (aOR 0.70, 95% CI 0.46–1.01). Prescription records don't confirm the patient was actually taking the drug, and clinically important differences can't be excluded.
articles.why: Fits with the newer Scandinavian guidance (Nov 16 issue) that relaxes routine CT for every DOAC head injury. Pharmacists should still confirm the agent, dose and last dose time, and have 4F-PCC or andexanet ready if CT shows a bleed.

articles.takeaway: Ceftriaxone alone prevented infections about as well as cefazolin plus an aminoglycoside for type III open fractures
articles.title: Ceftriaxone Compared to Aminoglycoside-based Antibiotic Prophylaxis in Type III Open Fractures.
articles.population: 156 adults with type III open fractures (34 ceftriaxone, 122 cefazolin plus an aminoglycoside), Banner Health hospitals in Arizona, 2017–2021
articles.summary: Surgical site infection by CDC criteria occurred in 12% with ceftriaxone vs 17% with cefazolin plus an aminoglycoside, a difference that wasn't significant (P = 0.60). Acute kidney injury rates also didn't differ (P = 0.74). The ceftriaxone group was small and treatment wasn't randomized, so the study can't show equivalence.
articles.why: A single 2 g daily ceftriaxone dose avoids gentamicin dosing, levels and nephrotoxicity in trauma patients who often get IV contrast. If your institution adopts it, ED pharmacists should still add anaerobic coverage (e.g., penicillin) for farm or soil-contaminated wounds and get the first dose in within the hour.

articles.takeaway: CRRT removed a meaningful share of diquat, more so with poor kidney function and early start, but kidneys did most of the work
articles.title: Contribution of continuous renal replacement therapy to diquat elimination relative to native renal excretion in acute diquat poisoning.
articles.population: 28 patients with acute diquat poisoning who kept making urine, 76 CRRT sessions, 1 Chinese ED/toxicology center, 2020–2025
articles.summary: Using mass balance, the authors compared diquat removed by CRRT with diquat excreted in urine during the same period. CRRT accounted for a median 46% of elimination per session, and its share rose as eGFR fell and as time from ingestion to CRRT start shortened. Across 120 hours, CRRT removal equaled about 22% of urinary excretion at the patient level. The study didn't measure clinical outcomes, so it can't say whether this removal saves lives.
articles.why: Diquat (and its cousin paraquat) have no antidote, so care is decontamination, fluids and extracorporeal removal. This supports starting CRRT or hemoperfusion early, especially if AKI develops; call poison control right away and avoid supplemental oxygen unless the patient is hypoxic if paraquat is possible.

articles.takeaway: A sepsis navigation tool was followed by lower death-or-hospice rates and faster antibiotics across 10 hospitals
articles.title: Impact of a sepsis clinical decision support system and workflow on sepsis-associated mortality or hospice discharge: A multihospital quasi-experimental study from 2018 to 2024.
articles.population: 631,620 adult hospitalizations (50,911 with sepsis), 10 Prisma Health hospitals in South Carolina, 2018–2024
articles.summary: The tool showed sepsis metrics, a real-time sepsis timer and shortcuts to documentation and order sets. After rollout, death or hospice discharge fell from 18.8% to 16.3% in sepsis and from 40.0% to 36.4% in septic shock, with adjusted odds about 27% lower in both (aOR 0.73). Monthly trends improved for sepsis but not for non-sepsis hospitalizations, which argues against a general secular improvement. Order set use, blood culture timing and antibiotic timing also improved; it isn't randomized, so other concurrent changes can't be ruled out.
articles.why: Antibiotic timing improved most when the order set was one click away. ED pharmacists can make sure sepsis order sets default to full loading doses, IV push beta-lactams where compatible and culture draws that don't hold up the first dose.

articles.takeaway: Haloperidol for ICU delirium didn't change cognitive function at 1 year, though missing data limit the answer
articles.title: Long-Term Cognitive Function Following Haloperidol Vs. Placebo Treatment in ICU Patients With Delirium.
articles.population: 624 adults with ICU delirium from the AID-ICU trial; cognitive testing in 134 of 343 survivors, 3 Danish ICUs
articles.summary: This prespecified follow-up compared global cognition (RBANS) 1 year after randomization to IV haloperidol or saline placebo. Median scores were 40 in both groups (mean difference 2 points, 95% CI −3 to 7), and executive function and domain scores didn't differ. Because only 39% of survivors were tested, best-case and worst-case sensitivity analyses pointed in opposite directions, so the authors call the result imprecise rather than proof of no effect.
articles.why: Haloperidol neither clearly helps nor harms long-term cognition, which fits the short-term AID-ICU results. For agitated delirium in ED boarders, use it for safety and symptom control at the lowest effective dose, check the QTc, and focus on nondrug measures and removing deliriogenic drugs.

articles.takeaway: A multifaceted stewardship program with monthly feedback halved antibiotics for respiratory diagnoses that never need them
articles.title: Effect of Ambulatory Antimicrobial Stewardship Intervention on Respiratory Antibiotic Prescribing in Primary Care Clinics.
articles.population: 20 intervention and 54 control primary care clinics, Prisma Health (South Carolina), Jan 2023–Mar 2025
articles.summary: Respiratory diagnoses were sorted into tiers where antibiotics are always, sometimes or never indicated. In intervention clinics, which got a multifaceted bundle that included monthly clinician feedback reports, prescribing for never-indicated diagnoses fell from 28.2% to 14.2%, while control clinics rose from 31.7% to 33.8% (adjusted OR for the interaction 0.32). Prescribing for sometimes-indicated diagnoses also fell, while prescribing for always-indicated diagnoses didn't change.
articles.why: The same tiered approach and peer-comparison feedback work in EDs and urgent care, where viral bronchitis and URIs drive a lot of unnecessary azithromycin. ED pharmacists can build tiered diagnosis lists into discharge order sets and share clinician-level reports.

articles.takeaway: COPD patients starting dupilumab had more new heart failure and AF than those on triple inhaler therapy alone
articles.title: Association Between Dupilumab and Risk of Cardiovascular Diseases Among US Patients With COPD: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
articles.population: 1,352 propensity-matched pairs of adults 40 and older with COPD on triple inhaler therapy, TriNetX US EHR network, 2024–2025
articles.summary: Patients who started dupilumab within 30 days of a COPD exacerbation were compared with those continuing triple inhaler therapy. Dupilumab was associated with more heart failure (HR 1.73, 95% CI 1.44–2.08) and atrial fibrillation or flutter (HR 1.57, 95% CI 1.24–1.99), consistent across sensitivity analyses and eosinophil subgroups. MI and ischemic stroke weren't significantly different. The authors stress residual confounding (sicker patients likely got the biologic) and don't claim a causal effect.
articles.why: A hypothesis-generating safety signal, not a reason to stop dupilumab. When a COPD patient on dupilumab comes to the ED with new dyspnea, keep heart failure and AF on the differential rather than assuming another exacerbation.

issues.note: A very thin Sunday window with no ED drug RCTs, so this issue runs short at 7 picks rather than padding. The EM items are an open-fracture antibiotic timing meta-analysis, sepsis fluid balance trajectories, frailty and mortality after stroke lytics, and adjunctive nicorandil with STEMI fibrinolysis. A drug anaphylaxis risk-factor study, a UK ICU stewardship audit and a CYP2C19/PPI cohort round it out; all are observational.
bottom_line: Pooled data couldn't confirm a safe time window for antibiotics after open fractures, but the four studies with validated infection definitions saw about 4-fold higher deep infection odds with delay. Keep cefazolin going in as early as possible.

Septic ICU patients who kept accumulating fluid on days 3–7 had about 30% higher adjusted odds of dying by day 28 (observational). Once resuscitation is done, stop reflexive maintenance fluids in boarding sepsis patients and concentrate drips.
In UK ICUs, a pre-set stop or review date on an antimicrobial order made a 72-hour review about 9 times more likely. It's an easy field to build into ED antibiotic order sets.

articles.takeaway: Antibiotic delay after open fracture wasn't clearly tied to deep infection overall, but rigorous studies saw about 4x higher odds
articles.title: Time From Injury to First Antibiotic Administration and Deep Infection Risk in Open Fractures: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.population: 24 observational studies of open fractures; 16 pooled (5,283 patients, 508 deep infections)
articles.summary: The authors kept time-from-injury and time-from-arrival studies in separate analyses because they measure different exposures. Neither stratum showed a significant link between delay and deep infection (injury-anchored OR 1.62, 95% CI 0.87–3.00; arrival-anchored OR 1.34, 95% CI 0.86–2.07), and no time cutoff could be estimated. The split between studies tracked how infection was defined: the 4 studies using a validated definition found OR 4.34 with delay, while 7 using an operative proxy found no effect (OR 0.86). That subgroup finding was post hoc and confounded, and overall certainty was very low.
articles.why: Absence of evidence isn't permission to wait. Keep weight-based cefazolin (2 g, 3 g if 120 kg or more) stocked in the trauma bay or automated cabinet so it goes in within the first hour, and document the injury time so delays can be audited.

articles.takeaway: Septic ICU patients who kept gaining fluid on days 3–7 had about 30% higher odds of 28-day death
articles.title: Association Between Daily Fluid Balance Trajectories and Dynamic Organ Failure Resolution (SOFA-2) in Sepsis: A Latent Class Growth Analysis of 16 262 Patients.
articles.population: 16,262 adults with sepsis who survived at least 72 hours in the ICU, MIMIC-IV database (US)
articles.summary: Daily net fluid balance from ICU day 3 to day 7 sorted patients into three patterns: steady low balance (85%), delayed decline after day 5 (8%) and continuous accumulation (6%). The steady group had the lowest 28-day mortality (20.8%) and the fastest SOFA-2 recovery. After adjusting for illness severity, loop diuretics and dialysis, the delayed group (aOR 1.30) and the accumulating group (aOR 1.27) had higher mortality. The authors treat the trajectories as markers of how sick the patient is, not proof that fluid itself causes harm.
articles.why: Fluid is a drug with a cumulative dose. For long ED boarders, pharmacists can flag maintenance fluids that keep running after resuscitation, concentrate antibiotic and vasopressor drips, and prompt a daily fluid balance check.

articles.takeaway: Frailty predicted 1-year death after IV lytics in older stroke patients, but it isn't a reason to withhold treatment
articles.title: Hospital frailty risk score and one-year mortality after intravenous thrombolysis in older patients with acute ischemic stroke.
articles.population: 423 adults aged 65 or older given IV thrombolysis for acute ischemic stroke, 1 center, 2014–2019
articles.summary: About 15% of patients had an elevated Hospital Frailty Risk Score (5 or more). One-year mortality was 34.9% in that group vs 20.6% in the low-risk group, and each additional point raised the hazard of death by about 8.5% after adjusting for age, comorbidity, NIHSS and ASPECTS (HR 1.085). Adding the score improved the prognostic model. The authors stress that the findings don't support withholding reperfusion.
articles.why: Frail older patients still benefit from tenecteplase or alteplase, so this belongs in goals-of-care and discharge planning, not the go/no-go decision. Pharmacists should still use an accurate weight for dosing and review antithrombotic plans before discharge.

articles.takeaway: Adding nicorandil to pro-urokinase lysis for STEMI was linked to better reperfusion and fewer 30-day MACE
articles.title: Adjunctive Nicorandil Ameliorates Cardiac Function and Clinical Outcomes Following Recombinant Human Pro-Urokinase Thrombolysis in Patients With Acute ST-Segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction.
articles.population: 116 adults with STEMI given IV recombinant pro-urokinase (62 with nicorandil, 54 without), China, 2024–2026
articles.summary: Successful reperfusion was 79% with nicorandil vs 61% without, and ST-segment resolution at 2 hours was 74% vs 56%. The nicorandil group also had lower troponin I and CK-MB at 24 hours, better ejection fraction and smaller LV diameter on day 7, and fewer serious arrhythmias and 30-day MACE. Adverse drug reactions were similar. Treatment wasn't randomized and the sample was small.
articles.why: Neither nicorandil nor pro-urokinase is available in the US, so this is hypothesis-generating. For US EDs without timely PCI, tenecteplase (weight-based, max 50 mg) plus aspirin, clopidogrel and an anticoagulant remains the regimen to have ready.

articles.takeaway: Asthma, NERD, food allergy and suspected beta-lactam allergy marked adults with a history of drug anaphylaxis
articles.title: Clinical patterns of suspected drug hypersensitivity and factors associated with drug-related anaphylaxis: a real-world study of 1,037 adults.
articles.population: 1,037 adults referred to a tertiary allergy clinic for suspected drug hypersensitivity, 2022–2023
articles.summary: NSAIDs (61%) and antibiotics (51%) were the most commonly suspected culprits, with beta-lactams named by 42% of patients. Urticaria, angioedema and bronchospasm were the most common reactions, and 25% reported drug-related anaphylaxis. Asthma (aOR 1.64), NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease (aOR 2.79), food allergy (aOR 2.76) and suspected beta-lactam hypersensitivity (aOR 1.81) were independently associated with an anaphylaxis history. It's a referred population, so the associations can't show cause.
articles.why: When an ED patient reports an NSAID or beta-lactam allergy, these comorbidities help separate a likely serious reaction from a low-risk label. Take a specific reaction history, keep IM epinephrine (0.5 mg) ready, and refer low-risk penicillin labels for delabeling.

articles.takeaway: Three-quarters of empiric ICU antibiotic orders followed local guidance; a set review date made 72-hour review 9x likelier
articles.title: Antimicrobial stewardship and resistance in intensive care units in the UK: a prospective national audit.
articles.population: 2,626 adults in 154 UK ICUs (point-prevalence survey with longitudinal follow-up)
articles.summary: Antimicrobials were prescribed to 61% of ICU patients. Of 2,116 empiric orders, 75% followed unit guidelines; 12% deviated after discussion with infection specialists, and 9.5% deviated with no justification or discussion. Review within 72 hours happened for 93% of eligible orders, and a pre-specified stop or review date was the strongest predictor of that review (adjusted OR 9.3, 95% CI 5.4–16.2).
articles.why: Antibiotics started in the ED often run unreviewed through a long boarding stay. A required stop or review date field in ED order sets is a low-effort, pharmacist-owned stewardship fix.

articles.takeaway: CYP2C19 metabolizer status wasn't linked to recurrent GERD documentation after starting a PPI
articles.title: CYP2C19 metabolizer phenotype and recurrent documented gastroesophageal reflux disease after proton pump inhibitor initiation: A cohort study from the All of Us Research Program.
articles.population: 21,135 adults with GERD, a definitive CYP2C19 phenotype and 1 year of follow-up after PPI start, All of Us Research Program
articles.summary: Recurrent GERD documentation in the following year occurred in 28%. Compared with normal metabolizers, adjusted risk ratios were 1.11 for poor, 1.02 for intermediate, 1.04 for rapid and 0.97 for ultrarapid metabolizers, none significant, and results held when limited to omeprazole. Further reflux testing or procedures were rare (1.2%) and also unrelated to phenotype. PPI dose and ongoing use weren't modeled.
articles.why: The authors say this doesn't overturn CPIC's advice to raise PPI doses in rapid and ultrarapid metabolizers. In the ED, CYP2C19 status matters more for clopidogrel choice after ACS than for a discharge PPI.

issues.note: A thin Saturday window with no ED drug RCTs, so this issue runs 8 picks. The EM items are a point-of-care DOAC level test validated in two EDs, a clinician review of semaglutide overdose, real-world low-dose alteplase decisions in stroke and a large pediatric ED influenza antiviral comparison. An opioid-free anesthesia RCT, a ceftazidime-avibactam combination meta-analysis, ampicillin-sulbactam hypokalemia and an HFpEF drug-class network meta-analysis round it out.
bottom_line: A whole-blood point-of-care test measured apixaban and rivaroxaban levels in a median of 14 minutes vs 73 for the lab anti-Xa assay, with strong agreement at the 50 and 100 ng/mL reversal and surgery thresholds. It could speed andexanet or 4F-PCC decisions once it's available.

Semaglutide overdose mostly means days to weeks of vomiting, dehydration and AKI because of its roughly 1-week half-life; there's no antidote and dialysis doesn't help. Hypoglycemia is the exception, mainly with insulin, sulfonylureas or counterfeit pens.
About 1 in 5 inpatients on ampicillin-sulbactam became hypokalemic, at a median of day 4. Recheck potassium around days 4–5 in patients over 75 or starting at 3.9 mEq/L or below.

articles.takeaway: A bedside test measured apixaban and rivaroxaban levels about an hour faster than the lab, with close agreement
articles.title: A bicentric pilot study of apixaban and rivaroxaban quantification using a novel point-of-care system in the emergency department.
articles.population: 69 DOAC-treated ED patients with paired samples, 2 EDs, plus a preliminary lab validation
articles.summary: Paired whole-blood point-of-care results were compared with a standard lab anti-Xa assay calibrated for each drug. In the ED cohort, correlation was 0.965 with a slope near 1 and a median bias of about −10 ng/mL. Agreement at clinical cutoffs improved as thresholds rose (kappa 0.62 at 30, 0.89 at 50 and 0.94 at 100 ng/mL), and precision was acceptable (CV under 6%). Median time to result was 14 minutes vs 73 minutes for the lab.
articles.why: Guidance often uses about 50 ng/mL (bleeding) or 30 ng/mL (urgent surgery) to decide on andexanet or 4F-PCC. A 15-minute level could prevent unneeded reversal in patients whose last dose was long ago; agreement was weakest at 30 ng/mL, so confirm low results before surgery.

articles.takeaway: Semaglutide overdose causes prolonged vomiting and dehydration; care is supportive and observation should respect its long half-life
articles.title: Recognition and management of semaglutide overdose and intoxication: a narrative review for clinicians.
articles.population: Literature through July 2026: trials, case reports, case series and poison center and pharmacovigilance data on semaglutide excess exposure
articles.summary: Most overdoses come from dosing errors, unit confusion with compounded multi-dose vials and products bought outside regulated supply. The main syndrome is gastrointestinal and protracted (nausea, repeated vomiting, abdominal pain, anorexia) because the half-life is close to a week, and volume loss, electrolyte problems and AKI drive serious outcomes. Isolated overdose rarely causes hypoglycemia, but it does occur with insulin or sulfonylureas, in people without diabetes and with insulin-containing counterfeit pens. Pancreatitis, euglycemic ketoacidosis, ileus and aspiration from delayed gastric emptying are less common but dangerous.
articles.why: Expect more of these as compounded semaglutide spreads: confirm the product and units (mg vs mL vs "units"), give aggressive antiemetics, fluids and electrolytes, check glucose based on co-medications, and use full-stomach precautions for sedation or RSI. Poison center input helps set the observation period.

articles.takeaway: Lower alteplase doses went to older, diabetic patients; worse outcomes reflected who got them, not the dose itself
articles.title: Clinician-Selected Alteplase Dosing in Acute Ischemic Stroke: Treatment Patterns and Adjusted Outcomes in a Taiwanese Registry.
articles.population: 418 adults with acute ischemic stroke given IV alteplase without thrombectomy, Taiwan, 2017–2022
articles.summary: Doses were grouped as low (0.46–0.64 mg/kg), medium (0.67–0.84) or standard (0.85–0.94). Each year of age raised the odds of a low dose (aOR 1.07), and diabetes was linked to medium (aOR 1.84) and low (aOR 2.71) doses. Good 90-day function (mRS 0–2) was 44%, 54% and 68% across low, medium and standard groups, but dose category wasn't independently associated with outcome after adjustment. Symptomatic ICH was too rare to compare.
articles.why: Low-dose alteplase (0.6 mg/kg) is still used in Asia, but this doesn't show it's safer or equivalent, and ENCHANTED didn't show noninferiority. Standard dosing (0.9 mg/kg, max 90 mg) or tenecteplase remains the default; pharmacists should use a measured or best-estimate weight rather than rounding down.

articles.takeaway: Baloxavir and peramivir cleared fever about half a day faster than oseltamivir in children seen in a pediatric ED
articles.title: Clinical features and comparative outcomes of antiviral treatment in children with influenza A and B: a propensity score-matched cohort study.
articles.population: 3,718 children with confirmed influenza A (1,717) or B (2,001) treated within 48 hours of fever, 1 tertiary pediatric ED in China, 2023–2024 season
articles.summary: After matching within each influenza type, fever resolved faster with baloxavir (about 1.5 vs 2.1–2.3 days) and peramivir (about 1.7 vs 2.2 days) than with oseltamivir. Differences in full symptom resolution were smaller and inconsistent. Recorded adverse events were 16.5% with oseltamivir vs 5.0% with peramivir and 3.6% with baloxavir, with no serious events. Influenza A brought more high fever and neurologic complications, and influenza B more GI symptoms.
articles.why: Relevant as flu season ramps up: single-dose baloxavir (approved in the US for ages 5 and up) avoids a 5-day oseltamivir course and its vomiting. Oseltamivir is still preferred for hospitalized, severely ill or very young children, and in pregnancy.

articles.takeaway: Dexmedetomidine-esketamine anesthesia slightly improved recovery scores, with less hypotension and nausea than sufentanil
articles.title: Opioid-free vs. opioid-inclusive anaesthesia in laparoscopic cholecystectomy: a multicentre randomised controlled trial.
articles.population: 315 adults having elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy, multicenter in China, 2025
articles.summary: Patients got opioid-free anesthesia (dexmedetomidine, esketamine and sevoflurane) or sufentanil plus sevoflurane, with NSAID and wound infiltration in both arms. The 24-hour overall benefit of analgesia score was better with opioid-free anesthesia (adjusted difference −1.3 points), but that was short of the 3-point clinically important threshold. Pain on movement and chronic pain at 90 days (16% vs 16%) didn't differ. Intraoperative hypotension (20% vs 36%) and postoperative nausea and vomiting (23% vs 34%) were less common without opioids.
articles.why: Supports ketamine-plus-alpha-2 agonist combinations as an option when you want to avoid opioid nausea or hypotension, but not as an across-the-board replacement. The same agents show up in ED analgesia and sedation, where subdissociative ketamine is already an opioid-sparing choice.

articles.takeaway: Adding a second drug to ceftazidime-avibactam didn't lower mortality in carbapenem-resistant gram-negative infections
articles.title: Ceftazidime-avibactam monotherapy versus combination therapy for carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative bacterial infections: a secondary meta-analysis of predominantly critically ill cohorts.
articles.population: 25 cohort studies, 2,676 adults with carbapenem-resistant gram-negative infections (about 82% in the ICU)
articles.summary: This reanalysis of an existing dataset found 30-day mortality of 31.2% with combination therapy vs 32.8% with monotherapy (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.79–1.04). Clinical cure, AKI and on-treatment resistance didn't differ significantly, and microbiological eradication was borderline (RR 1.15, p = 0.05). Polymyxin-containing combinations trended toward more nephrotoxicity (RR 1.28, not significant). All included studies were observational, so certainty is very low.
articles.why: Supports ceftazidime-avibactam monotherapy as a reasonable default for KPC-type infections, sparing patients polymyxin or aminoglycoside toxicity. Combinations may still make sense for MBL producers (with aztreonam) or very high-risk sources.

articles.takeaway: About 1 in 5 patients on ampicillin-sulbactam developed hypokalemia, usually around day 4
articles.title: Incidence of and Factors Associated with Hypokalemia During Sulbactam/Ampicillin Therapy: A Retrospective Observational Study.
articles.population: 182 hospitalized adults with normal potassium at the start of more than 2 days of ampicillin-sulbactam, 1 Japanese hospital, 2022–2024
articles.summary: Hypokalemia developed in 39 patients (21.4%), and 6 fell to 3.0 mEq/L or lower. Median time to onset was 4 days (range 2–13). A decision-tree analysis identified baseline potassium of 3.9 mEq/L or lower and age over 75 as the factors associated with hypokalemia. It is a small single-center study without outcome data.
articles.why: High-dose penicillins act as nonreabsorbable anions that increase renal potassium loss. For older patients started on ampicillin-sulbactam in the ED for aspiration pneumonia or skin infections, schedule a potassium recheck around days 4–5, especially with diuretics or low-normal baseline levels.

articles.takeaway: SGLT2 inhibitors and MRAs gave the most reliable benefit in HF with EF over 40%; no class lowered mortality
articles.title: Incremental associations of pharmacological components in heart failure with mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction: a systematic review and component network meta-analysis.
articles.population: 24 phase 3/4 RCTs in HFmrEF/HFpEF (LVEF over 40%); primary network of 10 trials and 12 regimens
articles.summary: For cardiovascular death or first HF hospitalization, incretin-based drugs (semaglutide or tirzepatide; HR 0.69), SGLT2 inhibitors (0.80), ARNIs (0.82) and MRAs (0.89) each showed incremental benefit, mostly from fewer hospitalizations. No class significantly reduced mortality. SGLT2 inhibitors and MRAs held up across most sensitivity analyses, while ARNI and incretin results were sensitive to trial selection and low certainty.
articles.why: Supports an SGLT2 inhibitor as the foundation, with an MRA added when potassium and renal function allow, for HFpEF patients admitted or discharged from the ED. Watch for MRA-related hyperkalemia in patients who come back with AKI.

issues.note: No ED drug RCTs this window, so the 8 picks lean on toxicology. Clinical Toxicology published three ED-relevant cohorts (naloxone infusions, massive GHB exposures, and kratom/phenibut/tianeptine), alongside a stroke meta-analysis on IV lytics before thrombectomy, a review of why sepsis steroid meta-analyses disagree, and ED opioid prescribing trends. An AJHP diagnostic stewardship study and an ICU infection-prevention meta-analysis fill out the rest.
bottom_line: About 1 in 5 ED opioid overdoses got a naloxone infusion, and fentanyl or opioid-plus-stimulant exposure tripled the odds. Long runs of dilute infusions added a lot of IV fluid, so concentrate the bag and reassess often.

In 154 massive GHB exposures, 75% arrived with a GCS of 3 and two-thirds were intubated, yet only 1 died and 27% went home straight from the ED. Supportive care works; an opioid on board raised the odds of hypotension about 4.5-fold.

Pooled RCTs still can't prove IV lytics add benefit before thrombectomy (functional independence 51% vs 48%, not significant), but the symptomatic ICH increase wasn't significant either. Keep giving lytics to eligible patients while thrombectomy is arranged.

articles.takeaway: Fentanyl and opioid-stimulant co-exposure tripled the odds of an ED naloxone infusion after overdose
articles.title: Factors associated with continuous naloxone infusion use following opioid overdose in the emergency department.
articles.population: 1,165 ED encounters for nonfatal opioid overdose treated with naloxone, 1 US academic center (Alabama), 2019–2024
articles.summary: A naloxone infusion was started in 227 encounters (19.5%), and infusion use grew over the study period. After adjustment, a fentanyl-positive screen (aOR 2.96, 95% CI 1.92–4.57) and combined opioid-stimulant positivity (aOR 3.00) were linked to infusion use, while a positive opiate screen made it less likely (aOR 0.50). Prolonged infusions sometimes delivered large volumes of IV fluid. The design is observational, so the associations aren't causal.
articles.why: Fentanyl-era overdoses are pushing more infusions. A common starting rate is two-thirds of the bolus dose that reversed the patient, given per hour; ED pharmacists can concentrate the bag to limit fluid, titrate to breathing rather than full alertness, and reassess within a few hours instead of running it on autopilot.

articles.takeaway: Massive GHB exposures caused deep coma and frequent intubation, but nearly everyone survived with supportive care
articles.title: Clinical characteristics and outcomes of massive gamma-hydroxybutyrate exposure in a multicentre emergency department cohort.
articles.population: 154 patients with whole-blood GHB of 300 mg/L or higher, 18 EDs in Victoria, Australia, Nov 2021–Mar 2026
articles.summary: Median GHB concentration was 380 mg/L, and 97% had other substances on board. Three-quarters had a first GCS of 3, 66% were intubated, 67% went to the ICU, a quarter were hypotensive and 20% needed vasopressors. Higher GHB levels predicted hypotension but not coma depth, and opioid co-detection was linked to hypotension (aOR 4.51) and hypoxemia (aOR 3.64). One patient died, and 27% were discharged directly from the ED.
articles.why: GHB coma is profound but usually short and reversible, so airway support and time are the treatment; there's no antidote, and flumazenil or physostigmine don't help. Watch for hypotension when opioids are also involved, and plan for withdrawal (which can need high-dose benzodiazepines or phenobarbital) in regular users.

articles.takeaway: Nearly a quarter of patients with kratom, phenibut or tianeptine exposure seen by toxicologists needed the ICU
articles.title: Clinical characteristics of unregulated psychoactive supplement exposures: a 15-year multicenter study of kratom, phenibut, and tianeptine.
articles.population: 152 encounters (97 kratom, 44 phenibut, 11 tianeptine) in the Toxicology Investigators Consortium registry, 2010–2024
articles.summary: Cases rose over time, and patients were mostly men (84%) with a median age of 35. Most use was intentional, for euphoria, self-treatment or managing withdrawal, and 48% had co-ingestants such as stimulants, opioids or other supplements. Overall, 23% were admitted to the ICU and one patient died. Only 10% got buprenorphine-naloxone and 10.5% got naloxone education or a prescription at discharge.
articles.why: These "gas station" products act on opioid or GABA receptors and don't show up on routine drug screens. Ask about them directly, treat kratom or tianeptine dependence like opioid use disorder (buprenorphine is an option), and send these patients home with naloxone.

articles.takeaway: IV lytics before thrombectomy nudged functional independence up 3 points, but the benefit wasn't statistically certain
articles.title: Intravenous thrombolysis prior to endovascular treatment for stroke: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
articles.population: 7 RCTs, 2,884 adults with large-vessel occlusion stroke eligible for IV thrombolysis within 4.5 hours
articles.summary: Functional independence (mRS 0–2) was 51.2% with IV thrombolysis plus thrombectomy vs 48.0% with thrombectomy alone (RR 1.07, 95% CI 0.99–1.15). A Bayesian analysis put the chance of any benefit at about 89%. Mortality was similar (RR 0.98), and symptomatic ICH was numerically higher with lytics but not significantly (RR 1.19, 95% CI 0.87–1.63). Neither superiority nor equivalence was shown.
articles.why: Supports current guidance to give tenecteplase or alteplase to eligible LVO patients without delaying transfer for thrombectomy. Stroke pharmacists should keep door-to-needle times fast and confirm the dose and time given before the patient leaves for the angio suite.

articles.takeaway: Sepsis steroid meta-analyses disagree mainly because they pool different trials; hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone consistently helped
articles.title: Discordant evidence on corticosteroids in sepsis: a meta-research study.
articles.population: 42 systematic reviews (2015–2025) covering 121 unique RCTs of corticosteroids in sepsis
articles.summary: More than half of pairs of reviews shared no trials at all, and only three pairs overlapped heavily. Of 38 reviews with a short-term mortality analysis, 39% found benefit and 61% didn't. The disagreement came entirely from reviews of broad, non-specific steroid strategies: reviews of hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone consistently found benefit, and those of hydrocortisone, vitamin C and thiamine consistently found none. No single methods factor explained the split.
articles.why: When a guideline or attending cites a steroid meta-analysis, check which trials it pooled. For septic shock needing ongoing vasopressors, hydrocortisone 50 mg IV every 6 hours (with or without fludrocortisone 50 mcg daily) has the most consistent support.

articles.takeaway: Median opioid dose per ED discharge prescription rose from 60 to 75 MME during the pandemic years
articles.title: Opioid prescription patterns from 2019 to 2024: a multicenter analysis in Maryland, USA.
articles.population: 117,912 adults discharged with opioid prescriptions from 13 EDs and 1 urgent care, University of Maryland system, 2019–2024
articles.summary: The study compared weekly morphine-equivalent dose per patient before and during the pandemic. Median dose per patient rose from 60 to 75 (p<0.001). Excluding buprenorphine and methadone, prescribing jumped in 2020 and then leveled off; including them, it kept rising every year, likely reflecting growth in ED-initiated OUD treatment. There were no indication or outcome data.
articles.why: Separating MOUD from analgesic opioids matters when tracking ED prescribing: rising buprenorphine is a success, while rising analgesic doses aren't. Pharmacists can audit discharge opioid quantities against a 3-day default and push nonopioid-first regimens.

articles.takeaway: Requiring an indication on urine test orders cut ordering 30% and raised appropriate tests from 61% to 85%
articles.title: Impact of implementing an indication-based urinary tract infection diagnostic order menu at a veterans affairs facility.
articles.population: Adults with urinalysis or urine culture orders at 1 VA medical center (Palo Alto), Jun–Nov 2023 vs Jun–Nov 2024
articles.summary: A pharmacy-led stewardship team replaced free-text urine orders with a menu requiring a clinical indication. Urine test orders fell by about 30% per month, and appropriate ordering in an audited sample rose from 61% to 85% (p=0.0004). Treatment appropriateness, C. difficile, repeat testing and 30-day mortality didn't change significantly. Only 8% of post-period orders citing altered mental status met likely-UTI criteria.
articles.why: ED urine cultures in confused older adults drive a lot of asymptomatic bacteriuria treatment. An indication-required order is a low-effort stewardship fix ED pharmacists can champion, especially for altered mental status without urinary symptoms.

articles.takeaway: Selective digestive decontamination cut ICU-acquired infections by about a quarter, but neither it nor probiotics lowered mortality
articles.title: Gut microbiome-based interventions to prevent ICU-acquired infections: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.population: Adult ICU RCTs, 2000–2025: 9 selective digestive decontamination trials (19,907 patients) and 29 prebiotic/probiotic/synbiotic trials (5,483 patients)
articles.summary: Neither approach reduced mortality (SDD RR 0.96; biotics RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.87–1.00). SDD reduced ICU-acquired infections (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.60–0.98) and halved pneumonia (RR 0.50), while probiotics didn't significantly reduce infections overall (RR 0.82). Prebiotics or synbiotics lowered pneumonia (RR 0.70). The two strategies were compared only indirectly, and the probiotic trials varied widely.
articles.why: SDD remains a debated, resistance-sensitive strategy, and routine probiotics for ventilated patients still lack mortality benefit (and carry bacteremia risk in the immunocompromised).
